#### Remark 6.14.

We note that the regularity condition on the $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word $\mathbf{v}$ is necessary in the current proof of Theorem 6.13. However, we conjecture that Theorem 6.13 holds for any $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word $\mathbf{v}$ , even without assuming that $\mathbf{v}$ is regular.

### 6.3. Irreducibility of Tilted Richardson Varieties

In this section, we use the tilted Deodhar decomposition to prove the irreducibility of the tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ (Theorem 5.11). We begin with the following definition.

#### Definition 6.15.

Let $\mathbf{v}=s_{i_{1}}s_{i_{2}}\cdots s_{i_{\ell}}$ be an $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v\in S_{n}$ . A distinguished subword $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ is called a positive distinguished subword if $J^{-}_{\mathbf{u}}=\emptyset$ . We denote such a subword by $\mathbf{u}^{+}$ .

The following lemma identifies the unique positive distinguished subword.

#### Lemma 6.16.

Suppose $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , and let $\mathbf{v}=s_{i_{1}}s_{i_{2}}\cdots s_{i_{\ell}}$ be an $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v$ . Then there exists a unique positive distinguished subword $\mathbf{u}^{+}\prec\mathbf{v}$ corresponding to $u$ .

#### Proof.

By definition, if $\mathbf{u}$ is a positive distinguished subword, its last factor $\mathbf{u}_{\ell}$ must satisfy

$$ \mathbf{u}_{\ell}=\begin{cases}s_{i_{\ell}}&\text{if }i_{\ell}\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(u),\\
1&\text{if }i_{\ell}\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(u).\end{cases} $$

Therefore, we can construct such a subword $\mathbf{u}^{+}$ inductively from right to left. This process is deterministic and produces a unique result. ∎

We now state the main result of this section.

#### Theorem 6.17.

For $u,v\in S_{n}$ , the tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ are irreducible.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ be a sequence such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , whose existence is guaranteed by Theorem 3.12. Let $\mathbf{v}$ be a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced subword for $v$ . By Theorem 6.13,

$$ \mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}=\bigsqcup_{\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\implies\overline{\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}}=\bigcup_{\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}}\overline{\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}}. $$

Let $Z\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}}$ be any irreducible component. Then $Z$ must be contained in one of the closures $\overline{\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}}$ . However, by Theorem 5.4, we know that $\dim(Z)=\ell(u,v)$ , and the dimension of each tilted Deodhar cell is given by

$$ \dim(\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}})=|J_{\mathbf{u}}^{\circ}|+|J_{\mathbf{u}}^{-}|=\ell^{\mathrm{word}}_{\mathbf{a}}(v)-\ell^{\mathrm{word}}_{\mathbf{a}}(u)-|J_{\mathbf{u}}^{-}|=\ell(u,v)-|J_{\mathbf{u}}^{-}|\leq\ell(u,v). $$

By Lemma 6.16, there exists a unique Deodhar cell $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}$ of maximal dimension $\ell(u,v)$ . Therefore, $Z\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}}$ . Since this holds for every irreducible component $Z$ , we conclude that $\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}=\overline{\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}}$ . As $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}\cong(\mathbb{C}^{\ast})^{\ell(u,v)}$ is irreducible, it follows that $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ is irreducible. Finally, by Theorem 5.11, the closure $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}}$ is also irreducible. ∎

### 6.4. Tilted Kazhdan–Lusztig R-Polynomials

In this section, we define and study the tilted Kazhdan–Lusztig R-polynomials $R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)$ (or simply tilted R-polynomials), which count the number of $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -points in the open tilted Richardson variety $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ . These polynomials generalize the classical Kazhdan–Lusztig R-polynomials defined in [30] when $u\leq v$ in the Bruhat order. See Section 2.4.1 for a discussion of the classical case. We present three equivalent formulas for this new family of polynomials (Proposition 6.18, Proposition 6.19, and Theorem 6.20) and conclude with several open questions. We begin with a direct combinatorial formula, which follows immediately as a corollary of Proposition 6.12.

#### Proposition 6.18.

Let $u,v\in S_{n}$ . The tilted R-polynomial $R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)$ is defined as

$$ R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q):=\#\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}(\mathbb{F}_{q}). $$

Then, for any $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , and any $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word $\mathbf{v}$ for $v$ , we have

$$ R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)=\sum_{\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}}(q-1)^{|J_{\mathbf{u}}^{\circ}|}q^{|J_{\mathbf{u}}^{-}|}. $$

We present a recursive formula, analogous to the original definition of classical R-polynomials.

#### Proposition 6.19.

Let $\left\{R_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}(q):u,v\in S_{n},\;\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}\right\}$ be the family of polynomial defined recursively as follows:

- (1) $R_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}(q)=1$ if $u=v$ ;

- (2) $R_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}(q)=0$ if $u\not\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ ;

- (3) If $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ , then

$$ R_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}(q)=\begin{cases}R_{us_{i},vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}(q),&\text{if }i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(u),\\ q\cdot R_{us_{i},vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}(q)+(q-1)\cdot R_{u,vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}(q),&\text{if }i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(u).\end{cases} $$

- (4) If $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)=\emptyset$ , then $R_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}(q)=R_{u,v,\flatten(\mathbf{a})}(q)$ .

Then, $R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)=R_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}(q)$ for any $\mathbf{a}$ such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ .

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from Proposition 6.18 and the recursive structure of tilted distinguished subwords. ∎

Finally, we provide an alternative formula for $R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)$ using the Hecke algebra $\mathcal{H}$ . See Section 2.4.1 for the definition and properties of the Hecke algebra $\mathcal{H}$ . For a tilted word $\mathbf{w}=s_{i_{1}}s_{i_{2}}\cdots s_{i_{\ell}}$ , define the corresponding element of $\mathcal{H}$ by

$$ T_{\mathbf{w}}:=T_{i_{1}}T_{i_{2}}\cdots T_{i_{\ell}}. $$

#### Theorem 6.20.

Suppose $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . Let $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ be $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced words for $u$ and $v$ , respectively. Then

$$ R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)=q^{\ell(u,v)}\cdot\epsilon(T_{\mathbf{v}}^{-1}T_{\mathbf{u}}), $$

where $\epsilon$ is the trace map.

We begin with the following technical lemma.

#### Lemma 6.21.

Let $x=s_{a,b}\in S_{a+b}$ be the bi-Grassmannian permutation defined in Definition 6.5. For any permutation $w\notin S_{b}\times S_{a}$ , we have

$$ T_{x}T_{w}T_{x}^{-1}=\sum_{w^{\prime}\notin S_{a}\times S_{b}}c_{w^{\prime}}T_{w^{\prime}}\quad\text{where each }c_{w^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]. $$

#### Proof.

Suppose there exists $y\in S_{a}\times S_{b}$ such that $T_{y}$ appears in the expansion of $T_{x}T_{w}T_{x}^{-1}$ . Without loss of generality, assume such a $y$ is miminal in the Bruhat order. By Proposition 2.19, it follows that $\epsilon(T_{x}T_{w}T_{x}^{-1}T_{y}^{-1})\neq 0$ . Therefore, to prove the original statement, it suffices to show that

$$ \epsilon(T_{x}T_{w}T_{x}^{-1}T_{y}^{-1})=0\quad\text{for all }y\in S_{a}\times S_{b}. $$

Since $x=s_{a,b}$ permutes the block $S_{a}$ and $S_{b}$ , we have $T_{y}T_{x}=T_{y^{\prime}}T_{x}$ for some $y^{\prime}\in S_{b}\times S_{a}$ . Since the trace is invariant under conjugation, we get

$$ \epsilon(T_{x}T_{w}T_{x}^{-1}T_{y}^{-1})=\epsilon(T_{x}T_{w}T_{y^{\prime}}^{-1}T_{x}^{-1})=\epsilon(T_{w}T_{y^{\prime}}^{-1}). $$

However, since $w\notin S_{b}\times S_{a}$ and $y^{\prime}\in S_{b}\times S_{a}$ , it is impossible for $w\leq y^{\prime}$ , so $\epsilon(T_{w}T_{y^{\prime}}^{-1})=0$ , which completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 6.20.

By the word property in Theorem 3.42, the elements $T_{\mathbf{v}}$ and $T_{\mathbf{u}}$ are independent of the choice of the $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced words, so we denote them by $T_{v,\mathbf{a}}$ and $T_{u,\mathbf{a}}$ , respectively. We will prove that the right-hand side of the theorem satisfies the same recursive relations as in Proposition 6.19. More precisely, we show that for any $u\sim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ ,

$$ R_{u,v,\mathbf{a}}(q)=q^{\ell^{\mathrm{word}}_{\mathbf{a}}(v)-\ell^{\mathrm{word}}_{\mathbf{a}}(u)}\cdot\epsilon(T_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{a}}), $$

by verifying all recurrence relations from Proposition 6.19. Recurrence (1) is immediate.

For recurrence (3), since $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ , there is an $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word $\mathbf{v}$ for $v$ ending with $s_{i}$ , so $T_{v,\mathbf{a}}=T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}T_{i}$ . There are two cases to consider:

- • If $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(u)$ , then there is an $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word $\mathbf{u}$ of $u$ ending with $s_{i}$ , so $T_{u,\mathbf{a}}=T_{us_{i},\mathbf{a}}T_{i}$ . Since conjugating by $T_{i}$ preserves the trace, we have

$$ \epsilon(T_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})=\epsilon(T_{i}^{-1}T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{us_{i},\mathbf{a}}T_{i})=\epsilon(T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{us_{i},\mathbf{a}}), $$

which proves the recurrence.

- • If $i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(u)$ , then using the Hecke relation $T_{i}^{-1}=\frac{q-1}{q}+\frac{1}{q}T_{i}$ , we obtain

$$ \epsilon(T_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})=\epsilon(T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}}T_{i}^{-1})=\frac{q-1}{q}\epsilon(T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})+\frac{1}{q}\epsilon(T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{us_{i},\mathbf{a}}). $$

The recurrence holds after multiplying both sides by the appropriate power of $q$ .

For recurrence (4), if $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)=\emptyset$ , then $v$ is $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable. Since $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , it follows from Lemma 3.31 that $u$ is also $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable. Then by Lemma 3.38, we have $T_{v,\flatten(\mathbf{a})}=T_{v,\mathbf{a}}$ and $T_{u,\flatten(\mathbf{a})}=T_{u,\mathbf{a}}$ , so the recurrence holds.

It remains to prove recurrence (2), which states that if $u\sim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ but $u\not\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , then $\epsilon(T_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})=0$ . We proceed by induction on $\ell_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathrm{word}}(v)$ . In the base case $\ell^{\mathrm{word}}_{\mathbf{a}}(v)=0$ , which corresponds to $\mathbf{a}=(1,1,\dots,1)$ and $v=\mathrm{id}$ , we must have $u\neq\mathrm{id}$ , and the statement is immediate. We now apply two reductions:

Reduction to $v$ is $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable: If $v$ is not $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable, then $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)\neq\emptyset$ . Take any $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ . By recurrence (4), we have:

$$ \epsilon(T_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})=\begin{cases}\epsilon(T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{us_{i},\mathbf{a}})&\text{if }i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(u),\\
\frac{q-1}{q}\epsilon(T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})+\frac{1}{q}\epsilon(T_{vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{us_{i},\mathbf{a}})&\text{if }i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(u).\end{cases}. $$

In either case, the right-hand side vanishes by the induction hypothesis, so $\epsilon(T_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})=0$ .

Reduction to $u$ is not $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable: Suppose both $u$ and $v$ are $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable. Then recurrence (3) gives:

$$ \epsilon(T_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})=\epsilon(T_{v,\flatten(\mathbf{a})}^{-1}T_{u,\flatten(\mathbf{a})}). $$

Since $u\not\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , we have $u\not\lesssim_{\flatten(\mathbf{a})}v$ by Lemma 3.31. The induction hypothesis then implies that the right-hand side is zero, so $\epsilon(T_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})=0$ .

Using the two reductions above, we may assume that $v$ is $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable but $u$ is not. Let $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}^{\prime}\mathbf{x}\mid$ be a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v$ , where $x=s_{p,q}$ is the bi-Grassmannian permutation as in Definition 6.6. Let $\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}^{\prime}\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{u}^{\circ}$ be the regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $u$ constructed in Construction 6.8, such that the first $\jump_{\min}$ entries of $u^{\prime}$ are increasing under the order $<_{a_{\jump_{\min}+1}}$ . Since $u$ is not $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable, we have $u^{\circ}\notin S_{q}\times S_{p}$ . By Lemma 6.21,

$$ \epsilon(T_{v,\mathbf{a}}^{-1}T_{u,\mathbf{a}})=\epsilon(T_{x}^{-1}T_{\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}^{-1}T_{\mathbf{u}^{\prime}}T_{x}T_{u^{\circ}})=\epsilon(T_{\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}^{-1}T_{\mathbf{u}^{\prime}}T_{x}T_{u^{\circ}}T_{x}^{-1})=\sum_{w\in S_{p+q}\setminus S_{p}\times S_{q}}c_{w}\;\epsilon(T_{\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}^{-1}T_{\mathbf{u}^{\prime}}T_{w}). $$

It remains to show that every term in the above sum vanishes. By construction, $\mathbf{v}^{\prime}$ is a $\flatten(\mathbf{a})$ -reduced word for $v^{\prime}$ , and $\mathbf{u}^{\prime}\mathbf{w}$ is a $\flatten(\mathbf{a})$ -reduced word for $u^{\prime}w$ . Since both $v^{\prime}x$ and $u^{\prime}x$ are $\mathbf{a}$ -flattenable, we have:

$$ v^{\prime}[p],u^{\prime}[p]\subseteq[a_{\jump_{\min}+1},a_{1})_{c},\quad v^{\prime}[p+1,p+q],u^{\prime}[p+1,p+q]\subseteq[a_{1},a_{\jump_{\min}+1})_{c}. $$

However, since $w\notin S_{p}\times S_{q}$ , we have $u^{\prime}w[p]\not\subseteq[a_{\jump_{\min}+1},a_{1})_{c}$ , which implies $u^{\prime}w[p]\not\leq_{a_{\jump_{\min}+1}}v^{\prime}[p]$ , and thus $u^{\prime}w\not\lesssim_{\flatten(\mathbf{a})}v^{\prime}$ . By the induction hypothesis,

$$ \epsilon(T_{\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}^{-1}T_{\mathbf{u}^{\prime}}T_{w})=\epsilon(T_{v^{\prime},\flatten(\mathbf{a})}^{-1}T_{u^{\prime}w,\flatten(\mathbf{a})})=0, $$

as desired. ∎

There are several natural questions related to the tilted R-polynomials.

#### Conjecture 6.22.

Let $u,v,u^{\prime}v^{\prime}\in S_{n}$ be such that the tilted Bruhat intervals $[u,v]\cong[u^{\prime},v^{\prime}]$ are isomorphic as posets, then $R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)=R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}}(q)$ .

In particular, in the case where $u\leq v$ and $u^{\prime}\leq v^{\prime}$ in strong Bruhat order, Conjecture 6.22 reduces to the combinatorial invariance conjecture (see e.g., [16, 10]) in type $A$ .

The next conjecture is an analogue of [16, Corollary 3.4].

#### Conjecture 6.23.

For a tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ , define the tilted Bruhat interval graph as the directed graph with vertex set $[u,v]$ and an edge $w\xrightarrow{e_{i}-e_{j}}wt_{ij}$ whenever $w\prec wt_{ij}$ in the poset $[u,v]$ . Here, recall that $w$ and $wt_{ij}$ are always comparable by Corollary 3.16. For any reflection ordering $\gamma$ of the set of positive roots $\Phi^{+}$ , we have

$$ R^{\mathrm{tilt}}_{u,v}(q)=q^{\frac{\ell(u,v)}{2}}\sum_{P:u\to v}\left(q^{\frac{1}{2}}-q^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{\ell(P)}, $$

where the sum is over all directed paths $P$ from $u$ to $v$ in the tilted Bruhat interval graph whose sequence of edge labels is strictly increasing with respect to $\gamma$ and $\ell(P)$ denotes the number of edges in the path $P$ .

### 6.5. Total Positivity of Tilted Richardson Varieties

In this section, we define the totally nonnegative parts of tilted Richardson varieties (Definition 6.26), provide an explicit parametrization (Theorem 6.28), and show that these spaces form CW-complexes (Theorem 6.33). We begin with the following definition.

#### Definition 6.24.

Let $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ be a sequence. The $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted totally nonnegative flag variety is the subset $\fl_{n}^{\mathbf{a},\geq 0}\subseteq\fl_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ consisting of all real flags $F_{\bullet}$ such that the Plücker coordinates

$$ \{\Delta_{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}}(F_{\bullet}):i_{1}<_{a_{k}}<i_{2}<_{a_{k}}\cdots<_{a_{k}}i_{k}\} $$

are either all nonnegative or all nonpositive, for every $k\in[n]$ .

#### Example 6.25.

If $n=4$ and $\mathbf{a}=(4,3,2,2)$ . Then a flag $F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ lies in $\fl_{n}^{\mathbf{a},\geq 0}$ if and only if the following groups of Plücker coordinates of $F_{\bullet}$ satisfy:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{4},\Delta_{1},\Delta_{2},\Delta_{3} \displaystyle\quad\text{have the same sign}, \displaystyle\Delta_{34},\Delta_{31},\Delta_{32},\Delta_{41},\Delta_{42},\Delta_{12} \displaystyle\quad\text{have the same sign}, \displaystyle\Delta_{234},\Delta_{231},\Delta_{241},\Delta_{341} \displaystyle\quad\text{have the same sign}. $$

We now define the totally nonnegative parts of tilted Richardson varieties.

#### Definition 6.26.

Suppose $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . The totally nonnegative parts of the tilted Richardson varieties are defined as

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}:=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}\cap\fl_{n}^{\mathbf{a},\geq 0},\quad\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\geq 0}:=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\cap\fl_{n}^{\mathbf{a},\geq 0}. $$

This definition is independent of the choice of $\mathbf{a}$ .

#### Proposition 6.27.

Definition 6.26 is independent of the choice of $\mathbf{a}$ so that the totally nonnegative parts are well-defined as above.

#### Proof.

We must show that for any two sequences $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{a}^{\prime}$ such that $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{\prime}}v$ , the following conditions are equivalent:

$$ \displaystyle\{\Delta_{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}}(F_{\bullet}):i_{1}<_{a_{k}}<i_{2}<_{a_{k}}\cdots<_{a_{k}}i_{k}\} \displaystyle\quad\text{have the same sign}, \displaystyle\{\Delta_{j_{1},\dots,j_{k}}(F_{\bullet}):j_{1}<_{a^{\prime}_{k}}<j_{2}<_{a^{\prime}_{k}}\cdots<_{a^{\prime}_{k}}j_{k}\} \displaystyle\quad\text{have the same sign}. $$

Since $u[k]\leq_{a_{k}}v[k]$ and $u[k]\leq_{a^{\prime}_{k}}v[k]$ , by Lemma 3.10, a Plücker coordinate $\Delta_{I}(F_{\bullet})\neq 0$ for a $k$ -element subset $I\subseteq[n]$ only if

$$ \#\left\{I\cap[a_{k},a^{\prime}_{k})_{c}\right\}=\#\left\{u[k]\cap[a_{k},a^{\prime}_{k})_{c}\right\}=\#\left\{v[k]\cap[a_{k},a^{\prime}_{k})_{c}\right\}=d. $$

If we sort the elements of $I$ under both the shifted orders $<_{a_{k}}$ and $<_{a^{\prime}_{k}}$ , we obtain

$$ I=\{i_{1}<_{a_{k}}<i_{2}<_{a_{k}}\cdots<_{a_{k}}i_{k}\}=\{j_{1}<_{a^{\prime}_{k}}<j_{2}<_{a^{\prime}_{k}}\cdots<_{a^{\prime}_{k}}j_{k}\}. $$

Then, the signs of the Plücker coordinates satisfy:

$$ \Delta_{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}}(F_{\bullet})=(-1)^{d(k-d)}\Delta_{j_{1},\dots,j_{k}}(F_{\bullet}) $$

so the two sign conditions are equivalent. This completes the proof. ∎

The totally nonnegative parts $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}$ are isomorphic to open cells, and they admit explicit parametrizations closely related to the tilted Deodhar decomposition. We state this parametrization in the following theorem.

#### Theorem 6.28.

Suppose $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , and let $\mathbf{v}=s_{i_{1}}s_{i_{2}}\cdots s_{i_{\ell}}$ be a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v$ . Let $\mathbf{u}^{+}$ be the unique positive distinguished subword of $\mathbf{v}$ corresponding to $u$ . Then the totally nonnegative part of the tilted Richardson variety $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}$ admits the following parametrization:

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}\cong\left\{gB=g_{1}g_{2}\cdots g_{\ell}B\;\middle|\;\begin{aligned} g_{j}&=\dot{s}_{i_{j}}&&\text{if }j\in J_{\mathbf{u}^{+}}^{+},\\
g_{j}&=y_{i_{j}}(\pm p_{j}),\text{ with }p_{j}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}&&\text{if }j\in J_{\mathbf{u}^{+}}^{\circ}.\end{aligned}\right\}, $$

where the sign $\pm$ in each term $y_{j}(\pm p_{j})$ is fixed in advance and depends only on $\mathbf{v}$ . Consequently, $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}\cong(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^{\ell(u,v)}$ , and in particular, it is homeomorphic to an open ball.

#### Example 6.29.

Let $u=4231$ , $v=3142$ , and let $\mathbf{a}=(4,4,2,2)$ be a sequence such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . A pair consisting of a regular $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v$ and the corresponding positive distinguished subword for $u$ is given by:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{v} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}\mid s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}s_{2}s_{1}\mid s_{1}, \displaystyle\mathbf{u} \displaystyle=s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}\mid 111s_{2}s_{1}\mid 1. $$

Then, the parametrization of $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}$ as described in Theorem 6.28 is given by:

$$ \dot{s}_{1}\dot{s}_{2}\dot{s}_{3}y_{1}(a)y_{2}(b)y_{3}(-c)\dot{s}_{2}\dot{s}_{1}y_{1}(-d)=\begin{pmatrix}c&0&0&-1\\
d&-1&0&0\\
ad&-a&-1&0\\
1&0&-b&0\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ .

To prove Theorem 6.28, we present the following lemma, which reveals the local structure of the totally nonnegative flag variety. For any $k,r\in[n]$ , define the $r$ -tilted totally nonnegative Grassmannian as the subset $\gr_{k,n}^{r,\geq 0}\subseteq\gr_{k,n}(\mathbb{R})$ consisting of all $k$ -dimensional subspaces $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that the Plücker coordinates

$$ \{\Delta_{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}}(V):i_{1}<_{r}<i_{2}<_{r}\cdots<_{r}i_{k}\} $$

are all nonnegative or nonpositive.

#### Lemma 6.30.

Let $U\in\gr_{k-1,n}(\mathbb{R})$ and $W\in\gr_{k+1,n}(\mathbb{R})$ be two linear subspaces such that $U\subseteq W$ . Define the set of all $k$ -dimensional subspaces between $U$ and $W$ as

$$ \mathbb{P}(U,W):=\{V\in\gr_{k,n}(\mathbb{R}):U\subseteq V\subseteq W\}\subseteq\gr_{k,n}(\mathbb{R}). $$

It is clear that $\mathbb{P}(U,W)\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{R})\cong S^{1}$ . Fix $r\in[n]$ . Then:

- (1) There exists a unique subspace $V_{1}\in\mathbb{P}(U,W)$ such that the data $\left\{\rank_{[i,r)_{c}}(V_{1}):i\in[n]\right\}$ is distinct from that of any other $V\in\mathbb{P}(U,W)$ . Similarly, there exists a unique subspace $V_{2}\in\mathbb{P}(U,W)$ such that the data $\left\{\rank_{[r,i)_{c}}(V_{2}):i\in[n]\right\}$ is distinct from that of any other $V\in\mathbb{P}(U,W)$ .

- (2) Suppose $U\in\gr_{k-1,n}^{r,\geq 0}$ and $W\in\gr_{k+1,n}^{r,\geq 0}$ . Then among all $V\in\mathbb{P}(U,W)$ , the subset of points lying in $\gr_{k,n}^{r,\geq 0}$ falls into one of the four configurations illustrated below, where red and solid markers indicate membership in $\gr_{k,n}^{r,\geq 0}$ : $V_{1}$ $V_{2}$ $V_{1}$ $V_{2}$ $V_{1}=V_{2}$ $V_{1}=V_{2}$

#### Proof.

We prove the case for $r=1$ . The general statement follows from this case by applying the cyclic rotation map $\tau^{r-1}$ , defined in Section 4.2.

We begin with part (1). Consider any flag $F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ such that the three subspaces $F_{k-1},F_{k},F_{k+1}$ are equal to $U,V,W$ , respectively. Fix all other subspaces of $F_{\bullet}$ , and allow $F_{k}=V$ to vary over $\mathbb{P}(U,W)$ . By Proposition 6.11 (2), the Schubert stratification of $\fl_{n}$ cuts this family of flags into two strata: a single point $F_{\bullet}^{\prime}$ and an affine line isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ . By examining the rank conditions defining the Schubert cells, the subspace $V\in\mathbb{P}(U,W)$ corresponding to the unique flag $F_{\bullet}^{\prime}$ is the special subspace $V_{1}$ . The subspace $V_{2}$ can be obtained in the same way by considering the opposite Schubert stratification.

For part (2), assume $U\in\gr_{k-1,n}^{\geq 0}$ and $W\in\gr_{k+1,n}^{\geq 0}$ . Then there exists a flag $F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ such that $F_{k-1}=U$ , $F_{k+1}=W$ , and $F_{i}\in\gr_{i,n}^{\geq 0}$ for all $i<k$ and $i>k$ . This follows from the known fact that $\gr_{k,n}^{\geq 0}=\pi_{k}(\fl_{n}^{\geq 0})$ , as stated in [54, Corollary 1.2]. One may construct such a flag by taking a preimage of $U$ under $\pi_{k-1}:\fl_{n}^{\geq 0}\longrightarrow\gr_{k-1,n}^{\geq 0}$ , and similarly for $W$ .

In this setting, whether a subspace $V$ lies in $\gr_{k,n}^{\geq 0}$ reduces to whether the corresponding flag lies in $\fl_{n}^{\geq 0}$ . Let $F^{1}_{\bullet}$ be the flag obtained by taking $F_{k}=V_{1}$ . By the classical Richardson stratification, $F^{1}_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{R}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ for some $u\leq v$ . Since $V_{1}$ is the special point in $\mathbb{P}(U,W)$ , it follows that $i\in\Asc(v)$ . Let $\mathbf{v}$ be any reduced word for $v$ . Under the classical Deodhar decomposition, the family of flags takes the form of one of the following two configurations:

$$ F_{\bullet}^{1}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}} \mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}1,\mathbf{v}s_{i}} \mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}s_{i},\mathbf{v}s_{i}} F_{\bullet}^{1}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}} \mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}s_{i},\mathbf{v}s_{i}} $$

The conclusion now follows from the parametrization of the Deodhar cells in Theorem 2.22 and their totally nonnegative parts in Theorem 2.24, based on the following observations:

- (1) If $F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}^{\geq 0}$ , then $\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}^{+}$ , and $F^{1}_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}^{\geq 0}$ . The first statement holds because only the maximal Deodhar cell $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}$ intersects $\fl_{n}^{\geq 0}$ . The second follows from the fact that the parametrization of $F^{1}_{\bullet}$ is obtained by removing the last factor from the positive parametrization of $F_{\bullet}$ in Theorem 2.24, which preserves total nonnegativity.

- (2) Conversely, if $\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}^{+}$ and $F^{1}_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}^{\geq 0}$ , then the set of points in $\fl_{n}^{\geq 0}$ must follow the desired configuration. This is because, in Theorem 2.24, the only allowed final factors in the parametrization are $y_{i}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})$ or $\dot{s}_{i}$ .

∎

Now we are ready to prove the main theorem.

#### Proof of Theorem 6.28.

Let $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}(\mathbb{R})$ . By the tilted Deodhar decomposition in Theorem 6.13, $F_{\bullet}$ lies in a unique tilted Deodhar cell $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}(\mathbb{R})$ . We proceed by induction on $\ell^{\mathrm{word}}_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ to prove the following two statements:

- (1) If $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}$ , then the associated subword $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ must be the unique positive distinguished subword $\mathbf{u}^{+}$ corresponding to $u$ ;

- (2) Moreover, if $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}(\mathbb{R})$ , then in the parametrization given by Theorem 6.13, $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ if and only if each Deodhar parameter $p_{j}$ has a fixed predetermined sign.

In the base case $\ell^{\mathrm{word}}_{\mathbf{a}}(v)=0$ , which corresponds to $\mathbf{a}=(1,1,\dots,1)$ and $u=v=\mathrm{id}$ , the statement is immediate. If $\mathbf{v}$ ends with a bar, then we may remove the final bar and work with $\flatten(\mathbf{a})$ in place of $\mathbf{a}$ , since $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ does not depend on the specific choice of $\mathbf{a}$ . The result then follows by the induction hypothesis.

The only nontrivial case occurs when $\mathbf{v}$ ends with a simple transposition $s_{i}$ . Let $\mathbf{v}^{\prime}$ and $\mathbf{u}^{\prime}$ be the words obtained by removing the last factor from $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ , respectively. Let $u^{\prime}\in S_{n}$ and $v^{\prime}=vs_{i}\in S_{n}$ be the associated permutations. Now consider the set of flags obtained from $F_{\bullet}$ by replacing the $i$ -th subspace $F_{i}$ with another subspace in $\mathbb{P}(F_{i-1},F_{i+1})$ . By the definition of tilted Deodhar cells in Proposition 6.12, we are in one of the local configurations depicted in Figure 15.

*Figure 15. Local configurations of flags in the tilted Deodhar decomposition obtained by replacing $F_{i}$ in $F_{\bullet}$ with another subspace in $\mathbb{P}(F_{i-1},F_{i+1})$*

We compare these configurations to those described in Lemma 6.30. The black bullet points in Figure 15 correspond to the special points $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ from Lemma 6.30, as determined by the rank conditions in Definition 4.1. Case (a) corresponds to the case $V_{1}\neq V_{2}$ , while case (b) corresponds to $V_{1}=V_{2}$ .

If $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}$ , then by Lemma 6.30, we must be in case (a), and $F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}}^{>0}$ . By the induction hypothesis, $\mathbf{u}^{\prime}\prec\mathbf{v}^{\prime}$ must be the positive distinguished subword, so $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ must also be the positive distinguished subword. This proves part (1).

For part (2), let $g^{\prime}\in G$ be the matrix representative of $F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ from the parametrization in Theorem 6.13. Then the parametrization of the flags in case (a) of Figure 15 is given by:

$$ g^{\prime} g^{\prime}\cdot y(\pm\mathbb{R}_{>0}) g^{\prime}\cdot y(\mp\mathbb{R}_{>0}) g^{\prime}\cdot\dot{s}_{i} $$

If $F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}}^{\circ}$ , then by Lemma 6.30, we have $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}}^{\circ}$ if and only if it is represented by $g^{\prime}\cdot y(\pm\mathbb{R}_{>0})$ (with a predetermined sign for the parameter) or by $g^{\prime}\cdot\dot{s}_{i}$ . Part (2) then follows from the induction hypothesis. ∎

Finally, we present the following lemma, which plays a crucial role in showing that the collection of cells $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}$ forms a CW-complex.

#### Lemma 6.32.

Let $\rho_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}:(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^{\ell(u,v)}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}$ be the parametrization from Theorem 6.28, defined in terms of the Deodhar parameters $p_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{>0}$ . Then any Plücker coordinate $\Delta_{I}$ of a matrix in the image of $\rho_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}$ is a polynomial in the parameters $p_{j}$ , with either all nonnegative or all nonpositive coefficients.

#### Proof.

By the Cauchy–Binet formula, the Plücker coordinate $\Delta_{I}$ is a polynomial in the Deodhar parameters $p_{j}$ , with each $p_{j}$ appearing with degree at most one. Since $\rho_{\mathbf{u}^{+},\mathbf{v}}$ maps $(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^{\ell(u,v)}$ into $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}$ by Theorem 6.28, it follows that $\Delta_{I}$ evaluates to either a nonnegative or a nonpositive real number for all positive inputs. Without loss of generality, we assume the sign is nonnegative.

Suppose, for contradiction, that some monomial in $\Delta_{I}$ has a negative coefficient. By letting the variables appearing in that monomial tend to infinity, and the others tend to zero, the value of $\Delta_{I}$ becomes negative, contradicting its nonnegativity. ∎

As a direct consequence of Lemma 6.32, we obtain the following theorem.

#### Theorem 6.33.

For any $u,v\in S_{n}$ , the totally nonnegative part of the tilted Richardson variety $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\geq 0}$ , stratified as

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\geq 0}=\bigsqcup_{[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]}\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{>0}, $$

forms a CW-complex.

#### Proof.

The proof is identical to the proof given in [50, Section 5], with Lemma 6.32 serving as a key ingredient in the tilted setting. ∎

There are several interesting directions in the line of research of total positivity.

#### Conjecture 6.34.

$\overline{\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{>0}}=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\geq 0}$ .

Conjecture 6.34 would imply that the face poset of the CW-complex in Theorem 6.33 is given by the interval poset of the tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ . We note, however, that the strategy used in [49] for the classical case does not apply here, due to the absence of a unique maximal element $w_{0}$ in the tilted Bruhat orders.

#### Conjecture 6.35.

The CW-complex in Theorem 6.33 is regular.

## 7. Connections to Quantum Schubert Calculus

In this section, we connect tilted Richardson varieties with quantum Schubert calculus. Specifically, we show that tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ are equivalent to the two-point curve neighborhoods $\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ in minimal degree (Theorem 7.3), providing an explicit geometric description of a new class of curve neighborhoods (Theorem 7.7). As a consequence, we derive an explicit formula for the cohomology classes $[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]$ in terms of Gromov–Witten invariants, and use this to prove a quantum analogue of the descent-cycling formula (Theorem 7.10).

### 7.1. Equivalence to Minimal-Degree Curve Neighborhoods

For $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ , let $\ev_{i}:\overline{M}_{0,3}(\fl_{n},d)\rightarrow\fl_{n}$ be the evaluation maps as defined in Section 2.3.2. Recall from Section 2.3.3 that the two-point curve neighborhood of degree $d$ is defined as

$$ \Gamma_{d}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})=\ev_{3}(\ev_{1}^{-1}(\Omega_{u})\cap\ev_{2}^{-1}(X_{v})). $$

The curve neighborhoods are the “quantum‘’ generalizations of Richardson varieties in the context of Schubert calculus. Understanding the expansions of the cohomology classes $[\Gamma_{d}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})]$ into Schubert classes would lead to a solution to the quantum Schubert calculus problem (Proposition 2.8). However, unlike Richardson varieties, very little in the way of explicit descriptions of $\Gamma_{d}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ was known [38, 14]. Here we provide a complete answer for the minimal-degree case $d=d_{u,v}$ .

We begin by introducing some definition used in the proof. The Bruhat graph is an undirected, weighted graph on the vertex set $S_{n}$ , where an edge connects $w$ and $wt_{ij}$ for each transposition $t_{ij}\in S_{n}$ . The edge is assigned weight $q_{ij}:=q_{i}q_{i+1}\cdots q_{j-1}$ .

The moduli space $\overline{M}_{0,3}(\fl_{n},d)$ admits a natural $T$ -action. The $T$ -fixed points of this moduli space can be described in terms of the Bruhat graph by the following lemma (see [22, Lemma 4.2]):

#### Lemma 7.1.

For any distinct $w,w^{\prime}\in S_{n}$ , there exists a $T$ -invariant curve $C\subseteq\fl_{n}$ containing both $e_{w}$ and $e_{w^{\prime}}$ if and only if $w$ and $w^{\prime}$ are adjacent in the Bruhat graph. Moreover, in this case, the curve $C$ is unique and has degree equal to the weight of the edge $(w,w^{\prime})$ .

Consequently, the $T$ -fixed points of $\overline{M}_{0,3}(\fl_{n},d)$ correspond to collections of edges (with multiplicities) in the Bruhat graph whose total weight equals $q^{d}$ , and which together form a connected tree.

We are now ready to prove the following proposition, which shows that the $T$ -fixed points in the minimal-degree curve neighborhood $\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ correspond precisely to the elements in the tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ .

#### Proposition 7.2.

For $u,v\in S_{n}$ , the set of $T$ -fixed points in $\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ is $\{e_{w}:w\in[u,v]\}$ .

#### Proof.

We begin with one direction. Suppose $e_{w}\in\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ . Then there exists a stable curve $C$ of degree $d_{u,v}$ passing through $e_{w}$ and intersecting both $\Omega_{u}$ and $X_{v}$ . Since $\ev_{3}^{-1}(e_{w})$ is $T$ -invariant, and every $T$ -invariant closed subvariety contains a $T$ -fixed point, we may assume that $C$ is $T$ -invariant. By Lemma 7.1, such a $T$ -invariant stable curve corresponds to a connected tree $C^{T}$ in the Bruhat graph. This tree contains $w$ , along with some $u^{\prime}\geq u$ and some $v^{\prime}\leq v$ , and has total weight $q^{d_{u,v}}$ .

Our goal is to construct a shortest path in the quantum Bruhat graph from $u$ to $v$ that passes through $w$ . If such a path exists, then $w\in[u,v]$ by definition of the tilted Bruhat interval. The construction proceeds in three steps:

- (1) Since $C^{T}$ is a connected tree, there is a unique path in $C^{T}$ from $u^{\prime}$ to $w$ and another from $w$ to $v^{\prime}$ . Concatenating them gives a path $P$ (possibly with repeated edges) from $u^{\prime}$ to $v^{\prime}$ in $C^{T}$ that passes through $w$ .

- (2) Replace each edge in $P$ with a shortest path in the quantum Bruhat graph between its endpoints. This yields a directed path $P^{\prime}$ from $u^{\prime}$ to $v^{\prime}$ in the quantum Bruhat graph that still passes through $w$ .

- (3) Since $u^{\prime}\geq u$ and $v^{\prime}\leq v$ in the strong Bruhat order, we can prepend a strong Bruhat path from $u$ to $u^{\prime}$ and append one from $v^{\prime}$ to $v$ , obtaining a path $P^{\prime\prime}$ from $u$ to $v$ in the quantum Bruhat graph that passes through $w$ .

We now claim that the weight of the path $P^{\prime\prime}$ is at most $q^{d_{u,v}}$ . The strong Bruhat edges used to connect $u$ to $u^{\prime}$ and $v^{\prime}$ to $v$ have weight $1$ , so they do not contribute to the total weight. Hence, $\wt(P^{\prime\prime})=\wt(P^{\prime})$ . Moreover, by Corollary 3.6, each subpath in $P^{\prime}$ has weight less than or equal to the weight of the corresponding edge in $P$ , and the total weight of $P$ is at most the total weight of $C^{T}$ , which is $q^{d_{u,v}}$ .

We remark that some edges $(w,w^{\prime})$ in the path $P$ may be used in both directions. However, this does not affect the total weight: in constructing $P^{\prime}$ , each such edge is replaced by a directed shortest path from $w$ to $w^{\prime}$ in the quantum Bruhat graph. Since one of the two directions, either $w\to w^{\prime}$ or $w^{\prime}\to w$ , has weight $1$ , each edge contributes at most once to the total quantum weight.

We now prove the other direction. Recall that in the quantum Bruhat graph, a strong Bruhat edge (denoted $\xrightarrow{1}$ ) is an edge with weight $1$ , and a quantum edge (denoted ${\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}}$ ) is an edge with nontrivial quantum weight. For any $w\in[u,v]$ , we claim that there exist two shortest paths, one from $u$ to $w$ and one from $w$ to $v$ , of the following form:

$$ \displaystyle u\xrightarrow{1}\cdots\xrightarrow{1}u^{\prime}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}\cdots\xrightarrow{q}}w, \displaystyle w{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}\cdots\xrightarrow{q}}v^{\prime}\xrightarrow{1}\cdots\xrightarrow{1}v. $$

We prove the claim for the first path, and the second follows by a similar argument. Begin with a shortest path from $u$ to $w$ in the quantum Bruhat graph. If the path contains a subpath of the form $x{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}}y\xrightarrow{1}z$ , then by Lemma 2.17, we may replace this subpath with an alternative path $x\to y^{\prime}\to z$ in the quantum Bruhat graph. Since both paths have the same total weight by Lemma 2.12, the only two possibilities for the replacement path are:

$$ x\xrightarrow{1}y^{\prime}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}}z\quad\text{or}\quad x{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}}y^{\prime}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}}z. $$

In either case, the number of quantum edges either increases or shifts further to the right in the path. This process must eventually terminates, yielding a path of the desired form.

Finally, we concatenate the two paths to obtain a shortest path from $u$ to $v$ that passes through $w$ , of the form:

$$ u\xrightarrow{1}\cdots\xrightarrow{1}u^{\prime}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}\cdots\xrightarrow{q}}w{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xrightarrow{q}\cdots\xrightarrow{q}}v^{\prime}\xrightarrow{1}\cdots\xrightarrow{1}v. $$

By Lemma 7.1, the subpath from $u^{\prime}$ to $v^{\prime}$ corresponds to a $T$ -invariant stable curve $C$ of degree $d_{u,v}$ passing through $e_{w}$ , intersecting $\Omega_{u}$ at $e_{u^{\prime}}$ , and intersecting $X_{v}$ at $e_{v^{\prime}}$ . Therefore, by definition, we conclude that $e_{w}\in\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ . ∎

We are now ready to prove the main theorem.

#### Theorem 7.3.

Let $u,v\in S_{n}$ , then $\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 7.2 and Theorem 4.4, $\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ share the same set of $T$ -fixed points. Since $\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ is $T$ -invariant and closed in $\fl_{n}$ , we have

$$ \Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})\subseteq\{F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}:\Delta_{w}(F_{\bullet})=0\text{ for all }w\notin[u,v]\}. $$

By Theorem 4.12, the right-hand side is precisely $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ , so we have $\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ .

Finally, by Theorem 5.4 and Proposition 2.8, both varieties have the same dimension:

$$ \dim(\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v}))=\dim(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})=\ell(v)-\ell(u)+2|d_{u,v}|=\ell(u,v), $$

and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ is irreducible by Theorem 6.17. Therefore, the two varieties must be equal. ∎

### 7.2. Cohomology Classes of Tilted Richardson Varieties

In this section, we compute the cohomology class of the tilted Richardson variety $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ (Theorem 7.7), which, by Theorem 7.3, coincides with the cohomology class of the minimal-degree curve neighborhood $\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ in the cohomology ring $H^{*}(\fl_{n})$ . By Proposition 2.8, it remains to compute the constant $c$ in Proposition 2.8.

Our strategy is to use path Schubert polynomials $\mathfrak{S}_{u,v}(x,q)$ introduced by Postnikov [46] (see Section 2.3.6 for more details). We show that there exists a monomial of the form $q^{d_{u,v}}x^{\rho-\beta}$ that appears in $\mathfrak{S}_{u,v}(x,q)$ with coefficient $1$ . This implies $c=1$ .

We say that a directed edge $w\to w^{\prime}$ lies in the tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ if $w^{\prime}$ covers $w$ in the poset $[u,v]$ . A directed path lies in $[u,v]$ if all of its edges lie in $[u,v]$ . We begin with the following lemma, which plays a key role in the construction of the special monomial in the path Schubert polynomial.

#### Lemma 7.4.

Let $u,v\in S_{n}$ and $i\in[n-1]$ be such that $u_{j}=v_{j}$ for all $j\in[i-1]$ . Among all directed paths in the tilted Bruhat interval $[u,v]$ of the form

$$ u=w^{(0)}\xrightarrow{t_{ip_{1}}}w^{(1)}\xrightarrow{t_{ip_{2}}}\cdots\xrightarrow{t_{ip_{\ell}}}w^{(\ell)}=u^{\prime} $$

with $p_{j}>i$ for all $j$ , there exists a unique path of maximal length $\ell$ . Moreover, this path is $x_{i}^{\ell}$ -admissible, and the $i$ -th entry of the final permutation satisfies $u^{\prime}_{i}=v_{i}$ .

#### Proof.

We construct the desired path via the following greedy algorithm. Starting with $w^{(0)}:=u$ , and assuming $w^{(0)},\dots,w^{(k-1)}$ have been chosen, we define $p_{k}>i$ to be the largest index such that the directed edge $w^{(k-1)}\xrightarrow{t_{ip_{k}}}w^{(k)}$ lies in $[u,v]$ . We terminate when no such $p_{k}$ exists.

Fix a sequence $\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\in[n]^{n}$ such that $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . The path is $x_{i}^{\ell}$ -admissible: the construction ensures that the transposed entries $u_{p_{k}}$ are strictly increasing with respect to the shifted order $<_{a_{i}}$ , so the indices $p_{1},\dots,p_{k}$ are distinct. Additionally, if $u^{\prime}_{i}\neq v_{i}$ , then the path could be extended by taking the next step from $u^{\prime}$ along the canonical shortest path from $u^{\prime}$ to $v$ constructed in the proof of Theorem 3.3, which would yield a further transposition $u^{\prime}\xrightarrow{t_{ip_{\ell+1}}}u^{\prime\prime}$ . Thus, we must terminate at $u^{\prime}_{i}=v_{i}$ .

We now prove that this is the unique maximal-length path of the given form. The proof is by induction on $\ell(u,v)$ . Suppose there exists another path of length $\ell^{\prime}\geq\ell$ :

$$ u\xrightarrow{t_{iq_{1}}}x^{(1)}\xrightarrow{t_{iq_{2}}}\cdots\xrightarrow{t_{iq_{\ell^{\prime}}}}x^{(\ell^{\prime})}, $$

We aim to show that $\ell^{\prime}=\ell$ and this path coincides with the greedy path. If $\ell=0$ , then the only possible path is the singleton $u$ , so the claim is immediate. If $p_{1}=q_{1}$ , then $w^{(1)}=x^{(1)}$ , and the induction hypothesis applied to $[w^{(1)},v]$ completes the argument. So we may assume $p_{1}\neq q_{1}$ . By construction, $p_{1}>q_{1}$ . Now consider the path

$$ u\xrightarrow{t_{ip_{1}}}y^{(0)}\xrightarrow{t_{iq_{1}}}y^{(1)}\xrightarrow{t_{iq_{2}}}\cdots\xrightarrow{t_{iq_{\ell^{\prime}}}}y^{(\ell^{\prime})}. $$

We claim that this path lies entirely in $[u,v]$ and has length $\ell^{\prime}+1$ , contradicting the maximality of $\ell^{\prime}$ . Let $\mathbf{a}$ be as before, with $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . Using Theorem 3.13, we work in the partial order $\leq_{\mathbf{a}}$ and verify the claim step by step:

- (1) For each $k\in[\ell^{\prime}]$ , we have $y^{(k)}=x^{(k)}t_{q_{1}p_{1}}$ , and $y^{(k)}\gtrdot_{\mathbf{a}}x^{(k)}$ . The first identity is immediate. The second follows from the assumption $u\lessdot_{\mathbf{a}}ut_{1p_{1}}$ and Proposition 3.15.

- (2) For each $k\in[\ell^{\prime}]$ , we have $y^{(k-1)}\lessdot_{\mathbf{a}}y^{(k)}$ . This follows from $x^{(k-1)}\lessdot_{\mathbf{a}}x^{(k)}$ and again by applying Proposition 3.15.

- (3) For each $k\in[\ell^{\prime}]$ , we have $y^{(k)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . This is proven inductively. Assume $y^{(k-1)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and $x^{(k)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ . It then suffices to show that

$$ y^{(k)}[j]=\max_{\leq_{a_{j}}}\left(x^{(k)}[j],y^{(k-1)}[j]\right)\quad\text{for all }j\in[n], $$

where $\max_{\leq_{a_{j}}}$ denotes the least upper bound in the lattice defined by $\leq_{a_{j}}$ . If $j<q_{1}$ , then $y^{(k)}[j]=x^{(k)}[j]$ . If $j\geq q_{k}$ , then $y^{(k)}[j]=y^{(k-1)}[j]$ . For $q_{1}\leq j<q_{k}$ , since the only values that differ in $x^{(k)},y^{(k)},y^{(k-1)}$ are among $\{u_{i},u_{p_{1}},u_{q_{k-1}},u_{q_{k}}\}$ , the statement reduces to

$$ \{u_{p_{1}},u_{q_{k}}\}=\max_{\leq_{a_{j}}}\left(\{u_{i},u_{p_{1}}\},\{u_{q_{k-1}},u_{q_{k}}\}\right), $$

which holds since $u_{i}<_{a_{j}}u_{p_{1}}$ and $u_{q_{k-1}}<_{a_{j}}u_{q_{k}}$ , and the intervals $[u_{i},u_{p_{1}})_{c}$ and $[u_{q_{k-1}},u_{q_{k}})_{c}$ do not intersect.

Therefore, the path from $u$ to $y^{(\ell^{\prime})}$ lies in $[u,v]$ and has length $\ell^{\prime}+1$ , contradicting the assumption that $\ell^{\prime}$ is maximal. This proves that the greedy path is the unique maximal-length path of the specified form. ∎

Denote the reverse lexicographic order (or revlex for short) as the monomial order on the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[q_{1},\dots,q_{n-1},x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]$ that compares exponents from left to right, where the first differing exponent determines the order, and the monomial with the larger exponent in that position is considered smaller. The following lemma shows that the leading monomial of $\mathfrak{S}_{u,v}(x,q)$ under this order appears with coefficient $1$ .

#### Lemma 7.5.

Let $u,v\in S_{n}$ . The leading monomial of $\mathfrak{S}_{u,v}(x,q)$ under the revlex order is of the form $q^{d_{u,v}}x^{\rho-\beta}$ with coefficient $1$ .

#### Proof.

We construct the path $P_{u,v}$ as a concatenation of $n-1$ subpaths $P_{1},P_{2},\dots,P_{n-1}$ , where each $P_{i}$ is the unique maximal-length $x_{i}^{\beta_{i}}$ -admissible path in $[u,v]$ , as constructed in Lemma 7.4. By construction, $P_{u,v}$ is an $x^{\beta}$ -admissible path from $u$ to $v$ .

Since $P_{u,v}$ is a shortest path from $u$ to $v$ , its quantum weight is $q^{d_{u,v}}$ by Lemma 2.12. The corresponding monomial in $\mathfrak{S}_{u,v}(x,q)$ is $q^{d_{u,v}}x^{\rho-\beta}$ , and it is the leading monomial with respect to the revlex order due to the length-maximality of each $P_{i}$ . Moreover, $P_{u,v}$ is the unique $x^{\beta}$ -admissible path, again by the uniqueness of each maximal-length $P_{i}$ . Therefore, this leading monomial appears with coefficient $1$ . ∎

#### Remark 7.6.

In the special case where $v=w_{0}$ , the path Schubert polynomial $\mathfrak{S}_{u,v}(x,q)$ coincides with the classical Schubert polynomial $\mathfrak{S}_{u}(x)$ . The leading monomial constructed in Lemma 7.5 corresponds to the bottom pipedream for $u$ , introduced in [2].

We are now ready to compute the cohomology class $[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]$ .

#### Theorem 7.7.

Let $u,v\in S_{n}$ . The cohomology classes $[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]$ and $[\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})]$ in $H^{\ast}(\fl_{n})$ both equal the minimal quantum degree component of the quantum product $\sigma_{u}\star\sigma_{w_{0}v}$ :

$$ [\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]=[\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})]=[q^{d_{u,v}}]\sigma_{u}\star\sigma_{w_{0}v}=\sum_{w\in S_{n}}c_{u,w}^{v,d_{u,v}}\sigma_{w_{0}w}\in H^{\ast}(\fl_{n}). $$

#### Proof.

By Theorem 7.3 and Proposition 2.8, we have

$$ [\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]=[\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})]=\frac{1}{c}\;[q^{d_{u,v}}]\sigma_{u}\star\sigma_{w_{0}v}=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{w\in S_{n}}c_{u,w}^{v,d_{u,v}}\sigma_{w_{0}w}\in H^{\ast}(\fl_{n}), $$

where $c\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is the degree of the projection map $\ev_{3}:GW_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})\to\Gamma_{d_{u,v}}(\Omega_{u},X_{v})$ . It remains to show that $c=1$ . Since $[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]$ expands integrally in the Schubert basis, each Gromov–Witten invariant $c_{u,w}^{v,d_{u,v}}$ must be divisible by $c$ . By Proposition 2.18, this implies that every coefficient in the monomial expansion of $[q^{d_{u,v}}]\mathfrak{S}_{u,v}(x,q)$ is divisible by $c$ . However, by Lemma 7.5, there exists a monomial whose coefficient is equal to $1$ , so $c=1$ . This concludes the proof. ∎

### 7.3. A Descent-Cycling Formula for Gromov–Witten Invariants

In this section, we present a descent-cycling formula for Gromov–Witten invariants (Theorem 7.10) as an application of the theory of tilted Richardson varieties.

Our proof differs from Knutson’s original approach to the descent-cycling formula for Littlewood–Richardson coefficients in [33], which is combinatorial and based on divided difference operators on Schubert polynomials. In contrast, our argument is geometric, relying heavily on the tilted Richardson varieties. It remains an open question whether there exists a combinatorial proof of the same identity for Gromov–Witten invariants using divided difference operators.

We also remark that a similar relation among Gromov–Witten invariants was established in [37]. However, their results and ours are independent and do not recover one another.

We begin by introducing some terminology. For $i\in[n]$ , let $\fl_{[n]\setminus{i}}$ denote the partial flag variety, consisting of nested linear subspaces omitting the $i$ -th subspace:

$$ \fl_{[n]\setminus i}:=\{F_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_{i-1}\subseteq F_{i+1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_{n}=\mathbb{C}^{n}:\dim(F_{j})=j\text{ for all }j\in[n]\setminus\{i\}\}. $$

Let $\pi_{[n]\setminus i}:\fl_{n}\to\fl_{[n]\setminus\{i\}}$ be the natural projection map that forgets the $i$ -th subspace $F_{i}$ of a complete flag $F_{\bullet}\in\fl_{n}$ . This projection $\pi_{[n]\setminus i}$ is a proper, flat morphism whose fibers are isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ . Define the divided difference operator $\partial_{i}:H^{\ast}(\fl_{n})\to H^{\ast}(\fl_{n})$ as the composition

$$ \partial_{i}:=(\pi_{[n]\setminus i})^{\ast}\circ(\pi_{[n]\setminus i})_{\ast}, $$

where $(\pi_{[n]\setminus i})\ast$ is the proper pushforward and $(\pi_{[n]\setminus i})^{*}$ is the flat pullback. We now state the following proposition, which describes the action of $\partial_{i}$ on cohomology classes of tilted Richardson varieties $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ .

#### Proposition 7.8.

Let $u,v\in S_{n}$ and $i\in[n-1]$ such that $[u,v]\cdot s_{i}=[u,v]$ . Then:

- (1) $\partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]=0$ ;

- (2) $\partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}]=\partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}}]=[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]$ .

#### Proof.

By Theorem 3.25, fix a sequence $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ such that $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and $i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(u)\cap\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ . We first establish the following geometric statements:

- (a) $\pi_{[n]\setminus i}^{-1}(\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}))=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ ;

- (b) $\pi_{[n]\setminus i}^{-1}(\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}))=\pi_{[n]\setminus i}^{-1}(\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}}))=\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ ;

- (c) The projection $\pi_{[n]\setminus i}$ restricts to an isomorphism over $\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}^{\circ}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}}^{\circ}$ .

For (a), it suffices to show that $\pi_{[n]\setminus i}^{-1}(\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}))\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ . Any $F_{\bullet}\in\pi_{[n]\setminus i}^{-1}(\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}))$ is either equal to some $F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ or satisfies $F_{\bullet}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ . If $F_{\bullet}=F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ , the result is clear. Otherwise, by Theorem 5.1, we have $F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}$ for some $[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]$ , or equivalently, $e\xrightarrow{y,\mathbf{a}}F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\xleftarrow{x,\mathbf{a}}w_{0}$ . Since $F_{\bullet}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ , Proposition 6.11 implies that $e\xrightarrow{y^{\prime},\mathbf{a}}F_{\bullet}\xleftarrow{x^{\prime},\mathbf{a}}w_{0}$ for some $x^{\prime}\in\{x,xs_{i}\}$ and $y^{\prime}\in\{y,ys_{i}\}$ . In either case, $x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\in[u,v]$ , so $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{x^{\prime},y^{\prime}}^{\circ}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ .

For (b), we prove only that $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\subseteq\pi_{[n]\setminus i}^{-1}(\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}))$ ,, as the other case is analogous. Let $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ . We aim to show that there exists $F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}$ such that either $F_{\bullet}=F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ or $F_{\bullet}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ . Since $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}$ for some $[x,y]\subseteq[u,v]$ , we consider two cases. If $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ , then by Theorem 3.23, we have $[x,y]\subseteq[us_{i},v]$ , which implies $F_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{x,y}^{\circ}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}$ . If $i\in\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ , then by Proposition 6.11 (5), there exists $F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ such that $w_{0}\xrightarrow{xs_{i},\mathbf{a}}F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}F_{\bullet}$ . Moreover, we have $e\xrightarrow{y^{\prime},\mathbf{a}}F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ for some $y^{\prime}\in\{y,ys_{i}\}$ , and therefore $F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{xs_{i},y^{\prime}}^{\circ}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}$ .

For (c), suppose for contradiction that two distinct flags $F_{\bullet},F^{\prime}_{\bullet}\in\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}^{\circ}$ have the same image under $\pi_{[n]\setminus i}$ . Then necessarily $F_{\bullet}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ . However, since both $w_{0}\xrightarrow{us_{i},\mathbf{a}}F_{\bullet}$ and $w_{0}\xrightarrow{us_{i},\mathbf{a}}F^{\prime}_{\bullet}$ , this contradicts Proposition 6.11 (4).

We now return to the main statements. For part (1), by statement (a), the projection $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\to\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})$ has fibers isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , and is not generically finite. Therefore, the pushforward vanishes: $(\pi_{[n]\setminus i})_{\ast}[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]=0$ , and hence $\partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]=0$ .

For part (2), we prove only $\partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}]=[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]$ , and the other identity is similar. By statement (c), the projection $\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}\to\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v})$ restricts to an isomorphism over the dense open subset $\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}^{\circ}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}$ , so the projection has degree one:

$$ (\pi_{[n]\setminus i})_{\ast}[\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}]=[\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v})]. $$

Then, using statement (b), we compute:

$$ \partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}]=(\pi_{[n]\setminus i})^{\ast}[\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v})]=[\pi_{[n]\setminus i}^{-1}(\pi_{[n]\setminus i}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}))]=[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}].\qed $$

The following well-known lemma describes the action of the operator $\partial_{i}$ on Schubert classes. It is a direct corollary of Proposition 7.8.

#### Lemma 7.9.

Let $w\in S_{n}$ and $i\in[n-1]$ . Then

$$ \partial_{i}\sigma_{w}=\begin{cases}\sigma_{ws_{i}}&\text{if }w>ws_{i},\\
0&\text{if }w<ws_{i}.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

This follows directly from Proposition 7.8 in the case $v=w_{0}$ , since $\mathcal{T}_{u,w_{0}}=\Omega_{u}$ . ∎

Finally, we state the descent-cycling formula for Gromov–Witten invariants.

#### Theorem 7.10 (Descent-Cycling Formula).

Let $u,v,w\in S_{n}$ and $i\in[n-1]$ such that $[u,v]\cdot s_{i}=[u,v]$ , and $ws_{i}>w$ . Then:

- (1) $c_{u,w}^{v,d_{u,v}}=0$ ;

- (2) $c_{u,ws_{i}}^{v,d_{u,v}}=c_{us_{i},w}^{v,d_{us_{i},v}}=c_{u,w}^{vs_{i},d_{u,vs_{i}}}$ .

#### Proof.

Part (1) follows from the Schubert expansion of the first equation $\partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]=0$ in Proposition 7.8, combined with Theorem 7.7 and Lemma 7.9.

Part (2) follows by comparing all sides of the second equation in Proposition 7.8:

$$ [\mathcal{T}_{u,v}]=\partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},v}]=\partial_{i}[\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}}], $$

combined with Theorem 7.7 and Lemma 7.9. ∎

## 8. Projections of Tilted Richardson Varieties

Let $\pi_{k}:\fl_{n}\rightarrow\gr(k,n)$ be the natural projection onto the $k$ -th flag. In [31, 32], Knutson–Lam–Speyer studied the images of Richardson varieties $\mathcal{R}_{u,v}$ under $\pi_{k}$ . Here we extend their results to tilted Richardson varieties. In particular, we show that

- • the image of any tilted Richardson variety under $\pi_{k}$ is a positroid variety (Theorem 8.5);

- • the restriction $\pi_{k}\colon\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\to\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})$ is birational if and only if $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v$ (Definition 8.6, Theorem 8.9).

We begin with a recursion for open tilted Richardson varieties.

#### Proposition 8.1.

For $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ ,

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}\cong\begin{cases}\bigl(\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}}^{\circ}\times\mathbb{C}^{\ast}\bigr)\;\sqcup\;\bigl(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\times\mathbb{C}\bigr)&\text{if }us_{i}>_{\mathbf{a}}u,\\
\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i}}^{\circ}&\text{if }us_{i}<_{\mathbf{a}}u.\end{cases} $$

Here we write $\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}$ to emphasize that it is empty if $us_{i}\nleq_{\mathbf{a}}vs_{i}$ .

#### Proof.

Since $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ , set $\mathbf{v}$ to be an $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $v$ that ends with $s_{i}$ . By Theorem 6.13,

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}=\bigsqcup_{\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}}D_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}. $$

Let $\mathbf{v^{-}},\mathbf{u^{-}}$ be obtained from $\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u}$ by removing the last letter (note that for $\mathbf{u}^{-}$ , the removed letter could be either $1$ or $s_{i}$ ). Then $\mathbf{v^{-}}$ is an $\mathbf{a}$ -tilted reduced word for $vs_{i}$ and $\mathbf{u}^{-}\prec\mathbf{v^{-}}$ . If $us_{i}<_{\mathbf{a}}u$ then every distinguished subword $\mathbf{u}$ of $\mathbf{v}$ ends with $s_{i}$ instead of $1$ . Therefore by the parametrization in Theorem 6.13,

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}D_{\mathbf{u^{-}},\mathbf{v^{-}}}&\cong D_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\\
gB&\mapsto g\dot{s}_{i}B.\end{split} $$

Since $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}\iff\mathbf{u^{-}}\prec\mathbf{v^{-}}$ , we have $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}\cong\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i}}^{\circ}$ under the map in (8.1).

If $us_{i}>_{\mathbf{a}}u$ , then by Theorem 6.13,

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}=\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}\\
\mathbf{u}\text{ ends with }1\end{subarray}}D_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\sqcup\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}\\
\mathbf{u}\text{ ends with }s_{i}\end{subarray}}D_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}. $$

If $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ ends with $1$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}D_{\mathbf{u^{-}},\mathbf{v^{-}}}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}&\cong D_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\\
(gB,p)&\mapsto gy_{i}(p)B.\end{split} $$

Otherwise if $\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}$ ends with $s_{i}$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}D_{\mathbf{u^{-}},\mathbf{v^{-}}}\times\mathbb{C}&\cong D_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\\
(gB,m)&\mapsto gx_{i}(m)\dot{s}_{i}^{-1}B.\end{split} $$

Since $\{\mathbf{u}^{-}:\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}\text{ ends with }1\}$ and $\{\mathbf{u}^{-}:\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}\text{ ends with }s_{i}\}$ are the sets of distinguished subwords of $\mathbf{v}^{-}$ for $u$ and $us_{i}$ respectively, using the maps (8.2) and (8.3), we have

$$ \bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}\\
\mathbf{u}\text{ ends with }1\end{subarray}}D_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\cong\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,vs_{i}}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}\text{ and }\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\prec\mathbf{v}\\
\mathbf{u}\text{ ends with }s_{i}\end{subarray}}D_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\cong\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{us_{i},vs_{i}}\times\mathbb{C}. $$

Combining these pieces gives the stated decomposition of $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 8.2.

For $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v,i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ and $k\neq i$ ,

$$ \pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})=\begin{cases}\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}})&\text{ if }us_{i}>_{\mathbf{a}}u\\
\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i}})&\text{ if }us_{i}<_{\mathbf{a}}u\end{cases}. $$

#### Proof.

We first claim that $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})=\overline{\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v})}$ . Since $\pi_{k}$ is proper, the image of the closed set $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\overline{\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}}$ is closed, hence $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})=\pi_{k}(\overline{\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v}})=\overline{\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v})}$ .

If $us_{i}<_{\mathbf{a}}u$ , then by Proposition 8.1 we have $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}\cong\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i}}^{\circ}$ via the map $gB\mapsto g\dot{s}_{i}B$ . Since $k\neq i$ , this identification does not change the $k$ -th flag, and hence $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{u,v})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}^{\circ}_{us_{i},vs_{i}})$ , which implies $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i}})$ .

If $us_{i}>_{\mathbf{a}}u$ , then by Proposition 8.1 we have

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}\cong\bigl(\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}}^{\circ}\times\mathbb{C}^{\ast}\bigr)\;\sqcup\;\bigl(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}\times\mathbb{C}\bigr). $$

Since this isomorphism does not affect the $k$ -th flag, it follows that

$$ \pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}}^{\circ})\,\cup\,\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}^{\circ}). $$

Moreover, $\mathcal{T}_{us_{i},vs_{i},\mathbf{a}}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}}$ , so taking closures yields $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,vs_{i}})$ as claimed. ∎

To prove Theorem 8.5, we also need a version of Lemma 3.31 where we flatten $\mathbf{a}$ from the back instead of the front:

#### Definition 8.3.

For $\mathbf{a}\in[n]^{n}$ , let $\jump_{\max}$ be the smallest index such that $a_{\jump_{\max}+1}=a_{\jump_{\max}+2}=\dots=a_{n}$ . Define $\cev{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{a})\in[n]^{n}$ to be the sequence obtained from $\mathbf{a}$ by changing the last $n-\jump_{\max}$ numbers to $a_{\jump_{\max}}$ .

#### Lemma 8.4.

If $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ and $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)\subseteq[\jump_{\max}]$ , then $u\lesssim_{\cev{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{a})}v$ .

#### Proof.

Since $u\sim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , we have $u\sim_{\cev{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{a})}v$ . It is then enough to check that $u[k]\leq_{a_{\jump_{\max}}}v[k]$ for all $k>\jump_{\max}$ . Equivalently, this is $u[k+1,n]\geq_{a_{\jump_{\max}}}v[k+1,n]$ for all $k>\jump_{\max}$ . Since $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , we have

$$ u[k+1,n]\geq_{a_{n}}v[k+1,n]\text{ for all }k>\jump_{\max}. $$

Since $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)\subseteq[\jump_{\max}]$ , $v_{\jump_{\max}+1}<_{a_{n}}\dots<_{a_{n}}v_{n}$ . Therefore by (8.4), $u_{k}\geq_{a_{n}}v_{k}$ for all $k>\jump_{\max}$ .

Since $u\sim_{\mathbf{a}}v$ , we have

$$ |u[\jump_{\max}+1,n]\cap[a_{n},a_{\jump_{\max}})_{c}|=|v[\jump_{\max}+1,n]\cap[a_{n},a_{\jump_{\max}})_{c}|. $$

Therefore for all $k>\jump_{\max}$ either $u_{k},v_{k}\in[a_{n},a_{\jump_{\max}})_{c}$ or $u_{k},v_{k}\in[a_{\jump_{\max}},a_{n})_{c}$ . Since $u_{k}\geq_{a_{n}}v_{k}$ , we can conclude that $u_{k}\geq_{a_{\jump_{\max}}}v_{k}$ , and thus $u[k+1,n]\geq_{a_{\jump_{\max}}}v[k+1,n]$ for all $k>\jump_{\max}$ as we desired. ∎

#### Theorem 8.5.

The image $\Pi_{u,v}:=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})$ is a positroid variety.

#### Proof.

We will proceed by induction on $t=|J_{\mathbf{a}}|$ . Consider the two base cases: $J_{\mathbf{a}}=\emptyset$ and $J_{\mathbf{a}}=\{n\}$ . In these two base cases, $\mathbf{a}=(a_{1}=a_{2}=\dots=a_{n})$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ is a (rotated) Richardson variety. By [31, Theorem 5.9], $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})$ is a positroid variety. Now suppose $t\geq 1$ and $J_{\mathbf{a}}\neq\{n\}$ . We claim that there is a chain of tilted Richardson varieties:

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\mathcal{T}_{u^{(0)},v^{(0)},\mathbf{a}^{(0)}}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{u^{(m)},v^{(m)},\mathbf{a}^{(m)}}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)},\mathbf{a}^{(N)}} $$

such that $\mathbf{a}^{(N)}=(a_{1}=a_{2}=\dots=a_{n})$ , $u^{(p)}\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}v^{(p)}$ for all $0\leq p\leq N$ and one of the following two conditions holds:

- (1) $v^{(p+1)}=v^{(p)}s_{i}$ , $\mathbf{a}^{(p+1)}=\mathbf{a}^{(p)}$ and $u^{(p+1)}$ is either $u^{(p)}$ or $u^{(p)}s_{i}$ as in Proposition 8.2 where

$$ i\in\begin{cases}\Des_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}(v^{(p)})\cap[\jump_{\min}^{(p)}]&\text{ if }p<m\\ \Des_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}(v^{(p)})\cap[\jump_{\max}^{(p)}+1,n]&\text{ if }p\geq m.\end{cases} $$

and $\jump_{\min}^{(p)}=\min\{i<n:\mathbf{a}^{(p)}_{i}\neq\mathbf{a}^{(p)}_{i+1}\}$ and $\jump_{\max}^{(p)}=\max\{i<n:\mathbf{a}^{(p)}_{i}\neq\mathbf{a}^{(p)}_{i+1}\}$ .

- (2) $u^{(p+1)}=u^{(p)},v^{(p+1)}=v^{(p)}$ and

$$ \mathbf{a}^{(p+1)}=\begin{cases}\flatten(\mathbf{a}^{(p)})&\text{ if }p<m\\ \cev{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{a}^{(p)})&\text{ if }p\geq m.\end{cases} $$

In particular, by Proposition 8.2, Lemma 8.4 and Lemma 3.31,

$$ \pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p-1)},v^{(p-1)}})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)}})\text{ for all }p\in[N], $$

hence $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})$ is a positroid variety by the base cases.

Let us explain how to obtain such a chain of tilted Richardson varieties. If $\jump_{t_{p}}^{(p)}\leq k$ , we can keep applying Proposition 8.2 as long as $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)\cap[\jump_{\min}^{(p)}]\neq\emptyset$ . Each of these steps is of the form (1). Now if $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)\cap[\jump_{t_{p}}^{(p)}]=\emptyset$ , then by Lemma 3.31, $u\lesssim_{\flatten(\mathbf{a})}v$ and $\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)},\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}=\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)},\flatten(\mathbf{a}^{(p)})}$ and we set $u^{(p+1)}=u^{(p)},v^{(p+1)}=v^{(p)}$ and $\mathbf{a}^{(p+1)}=\flatten(\mathbf{a}^{(p)})$ as in case (2). Since $\jump_{\min}$ increases every time we flatten $\mathbf{a}^{(p)}$ , there will come a time where $\jump_{\min}^{(p)}>k$ . We set $m$ to be the index of the first time this happens.

Now for $p\geq m$ , we similarly apply Proposition 8.2 until $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)\cap[\jump_{\max}^{(p)}+1,n]=\emptyset$ . Then by Lemma 8.4, we flatten $\mathbf{a}$ from the back and reduce $|J_{\mathbf{a}}|$ without changing $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})$ . This process will end once $J_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}\subseteq\{n\}$ and we obtain the chain in (8.5) as desired. ∎

#### Definition 8.6.

For $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v\in S_{n}$ , we say $u$ is less than or equals $v$ in $k$ -tilted Bruhat order (denoted as $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v$ ) if there exists a shortest path in $\Gamma_{n}$

$$ u=w^{(0)}\xrightarrow{t_{c_{1},d_{1}}}w^{(1)}\xrightarrow{t_{c_{2},d_{2}}}\dots\xrightarrow{t_{c_{\ell},d_{\ell}}}w^{(\ell)}=v $$

such that $c_{j}\leq k<d_{j}$ for all $j\in[\ell]$ .

#### Remark 8.7.

In the case where $u\leq v$ in strong Bruhat order, the $k$ -tilted Bruhat order is equivalent to the $k$ -Bruhat order first appeared in [35] and studied extensively in [3].

#### Lemma 8.8.

For $u\lesssim_{\mathbf{a}}v,i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(v)$ and $i\neq k$ , we have

- (1) if $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v$ then $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(u)$ .

- (2) if $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(u)$ , then $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v$ if and only if $us_{i}\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}vs_{i}$ .

#### Proof.

We first prove (1). For $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v$ , let $u=w^{(0)}\xrightarrow{t_{c_{1},d_{1}}}w^{(1)}\xrightarrow{t_{c_{2},d_{2}}}\dots\xrightarrow{t_{c_{\ell},d_{\ell}}}w^{(\ell)}=v$ be as in (8.6). We claim that $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w^{(j)})$ for all $j\in[\ell]$ . Suppose $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w^{(j)})$ for some $j$ , by the lifting property (Theorem 3.23), either $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w^{(j-1)})$ or $w^{(j)}s_{i},w^{(j-1)}s_{i}\in[w^{(j-1)},w^{(j)}]$ . Since $[w^{(j-1)},w^{(j)}]$ is a rank $1$ interval, the latter implies that $w^{(j)}=w^{(j-1)}s_{i}$ , impossible if $i\neq k$ . Therefore $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w^{(j-1)})$ and we are done by induction.

For ( $\implies$ ) direction of (2), if $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v$ , then by part (1), $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w^{(j)})$ for all $0\leq j\leq\ell$ . We claim that

$$ us_{i}=w^{(0)}s_{i}\xrightarrow{t_{c^{\prime}_{1},d^{\prime}_{1}}}w^{(1)}s_{i}\xrightarrow{t_{c^{\prime}_{2},d^{\prime}_{2}}}\dots\xrightarrow{t_{c^{\prime}_{\ell},d^{\prime}_{\ell}}}w^{(\ell)}s_{i}=vs_{i} $$

is a shortest path on $\Gamma_{n}$ such that $c^{\prime}_{j}\leq k<d^{\prime}_{j}$ for all $j\in[\ell]$ . By the lifting property (Theorem 3.23), $w^{(j)}s_{i}\in[w^{(j-1)}s_{i},w^{(j)}]$ . Consider the rank $2$ interval $[w^{(j-1)}s_{i},w^{(j)}]$ as in Figure 16, we have $t_{c_{j}^{\prime},d_{j}^{\prime}}=s_{i}t_{c_{j},d_{j}}s_{i}$ . Since $i\neq k$ , it is straightforward to see that $c^{\prime}_{j}\leq k<d^{\prime}_{j}$ . Therefore (8.7) produces a chain from $us_{i}$ to $vs_{i}$ as in Definition 8.6 and we can conclude that $us_{i}\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}vs_{i}$ .

*Figure 16. The tilted Bruhat interval $[us_{i},ut_{a,b}]$*

The ( $\impliedby$ ) direction of (2) follows by similar reasoning, replacing $\Des_{\mathbf{a}}(w^{(j)})$ with $\Asc_{\mathbf{a}}(w^{(j)})$ whenever necessary. ∎

Motivated by the connection between $k$ -Bruhat orders and projections of Richardson varieties [31, 32], we prove a generalization to all tilted Richardson varieties.

#### Theorem 8.9.

The map $\pi_{k}:\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\rightarrow\Pi_{u,v}$ is birational if and only if $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v$ .

#### Proof.

If $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ is a Richardson variety, this is [32, Corollary 3.4]. Similarly, if $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ is a rotated Richardson variety, then $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}v$ where $\mathbf{a}=(a,\dots,a)$ for some $a\in[n]$ . Equivalently, $\tau^{-a+1}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v})=\mathcal{T}_{\tau^{-a+1}u,\tau^{-a+1}v}$ is a Richardson variety. Since $\Gamma_{n}$ is invariant under left multiplication by $\tau$ , $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v\iff\tau^{-a+1}u\leq_{(1,\dots,1)}^{k}\tau^{-a+1}v$ . Since $\tau$ commutes with $\pi_{k}$ and $\tau$ sends a positroid variety to a positroid variety, Theorem 8.9 holds in this case.

Now when $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ is not a (rotated) Richardson variety, as in the proof of Theorem 8.5, there exists a chain of tilted Richardson varieties

$$ \mathcal{T}_{u,v}=\mathcal{T}_{u^{(0)},v^{(0)}}\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{u^{(1)},v^{(1)}}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}} $$

such that $\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}}$ is a rotated Richardson variety and $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)}})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)}})$ for all $p<N$ as in Proposition 8.2.

( $\implies$ ): Notice that by Proposition 8.2, $\dim(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)}})\geq\dim(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)}})$ and that by the construction in (8.5), equality holds if and only if one of the following holds:

- (1) $(u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)})=(u^{(p)},v^{(p)})$ ;

- (2) $(u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)})=(u^{(p)}s_{i},v^{(p)}s_{i})$ where $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}(v^{(p)})\cap\Des_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}(u^{(p)})$ and $i\neq k$ .

Therefore $\pi_{k}$ is birational on $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ if and only if each step in the chain of tilted Richardsons must be one of the two cases above and $u^{(N)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{(N)}}^{k}v^{(N)}$ . By (2) of Lemma 8.8, $\pi_{k}$ is birational implies $u\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v$ .

( $\impliedby$ ): For any step in (8.8) where $(u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)})\neq(u^{(p)},v^{(p)})$ , we have $v^{(p+1)}=v^{(p)}s_{i}$ with $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}(v^{(p)})$ . By (1) of Lemma 8.8, $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}(u^{(p)})$ and thus $u^{(p+1)}=u^{(p)}s_{i}$ . In particular, $\dim(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)}})=\dim(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)}})$ and $\pi_{k}$ is birational on $\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)}}$ if and only if it is birational on $\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)}}$ . Therefore by (2) of Lemma 8.8, $u^{(p)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}^{k}v^{(p)}$ implies $u^{(p+1)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{(p+1)}}^{k}v^{(p+1)}$ . Since $\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}$ is independent of the choice of $\mathbf{a}$ , we also have $u^{(p)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}^{k}v^{(p)}$ implies $u^{(p+1)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{(p+1)}}^{k}v^{(p+1)}$ when $(u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)})=(u^{(p)},v^{(p)})$ . Since $u=u^{(0)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}}^{k}v^{(0)}=v$ , we can conclude that $u^{(N)}\leq_{\mathbf{a}^{(N)}}^{k}v^{(N)}$ . Therefore $\pi_{k}$ is birational on $\mathcal{T}_{u,v}$ . ∎

#### Theorem 8.10.

If $\pi_{k}:\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\rightarrow\Pi_{u,v}$ is birational, then $\pi_{k}:\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ}\rightarrow\Pi_{u,v}^{\circ}$ is an isomorphism.

#### Proof.

We will show that if $\pi_{k}:\mathcal{T}_{u,v}\rightarrow\Pi_{u,v}$ is birational, then there exists a rotated Richardson variety $\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}}$ such that

$$ \pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}}^{\circ})=\Pi_{u,v}^{\circ}. $$

By the “ $\implies$ ” part in the proof of Theorem 8.9, there exists a chain of tilted Richardson varieties of the form (8.8) such that

- • $\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}}$ is a rotated Richardson variety,

- • $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}})=\Pi_{u,v}$ ,

and, for all $p<N$ , either

- (1) $(u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)})=(u^{(p)},v^{(p)})$ ; or

- (2) $(u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)})=(u^{(p)}s_{i},v^{(p)}s_{i})$ where $i\in\Des_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}(v^{(p)})\cap\Des_{\mathbf{a}^{(p)}}(u^{(p)})$ and $i\neq k$ .

Notice that in case (1), we automatically have $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)}}^{\circ})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)}}^{\circ})$ . In case (2), by Proposition 8.1, $\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)}}^{\circ}\cong\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)}s_{i},v^{(p)}s_{i}}^{\circ}$ under the map $gB\mapsto g\dot{s}_{i}B$ . Since $i\neq k$ , we have $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)}}^{\circ})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)}}^{\circ})$ . Therefore $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p+1)},v^{(p+1)}}^{\circ})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(p)},v^{(p)}}^{\circ})$ for all $p<N$ and thus $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ})=\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}}^{\circ})$ .

Since $\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}}$ is a rotated Richardson variety, $u^{(N)}\leq^{k}_{\mathbf{a}}v^{(N)}$ where $\mathbf{a}=(a,a,\dots,a)$ for some $a$ . Since the quantum Bruhat graph $\Gamma_{n}$ is invariant under left multiplication by the long cycle $\tau=23\cdots 1$ (Lemma 2.11), we have $\tau^{-a+1}u^{(N)}\leq\tau^{-a+1}v^{(N)}$ in $k$ -Bruhat order. Since the cyclic rotation $\tau$ commutes with $\pi_{k}$ , by [31, Theorem 5.9], $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u^{(N)},v^{(N)}}^{\circ})=\Pi_{u,v}^{\circ}$ . We can then conclude that $\pi_{k}(\mathcal{T}_{u,v}^{\circ})=\Pi_{u,v}^{\circ}$ as desired. ∎
